findings.rationale: The two claims both establish minimum character length requirements for memorized secrets (passwords), but for different contexts. Claim A requires at least 6 characters for randomly chosen secrets, while Claim B requires a minimum of 15 characters for passwords used in single-factor authentication. When a password is used as single-factor authentication (as described in Claim B), it falls within the scope of both claims—making the requirements irreconcilable: the same entity cannot simultaneously comply with both a 6-character minimum and a 15-character minimum for the same type of credential in the same authentication context.
findings.resolution_hint: Claim B likely supersedes or refines Claim A for the specific case of single-factor authentication, establishing the stricter 15-character requirement as the controlling standard for that use case.

findings.subject: look-up secrets
findings.rationale: Both claims address the secure delivery of look-up secrets online and invoke post-enrollment binding requirements, but they reference different sections: Section 6.1.2 (Claim A) versus Section 4.1.2 (Claim B). This suggests incompatible normative frameworks or standards, as they cannot both be the controlling requirement for the same subject matter.
findings.resolution_hint: Clarify which section (4.1.2 or 6.1.2) contains the actual binding requirement, or whether these apply to different contexts.

a.evidence_quote: If distributed online, look-up secrets SHALL be distributed over a secure channel in accordance with the post-enrollment binding requirements in Section 6.1.2
